name: Japanese Woodblock Prints
intro: Ukiyo-e, “pictures of the floating world,” were sold as woodblock prints from the 1680s into the 1880s. They were first made in Edo, the city now called Tokyo. Publishers issued them in quantity for the city's townspeople. The most common subjects were courtesans and actors of kabuki, a theater of dance and drama; landscape came later. Each print took four people: a designer, a block carver, a printer and the publisher who issued it for sale.
homeDescription: How to recognize a Japanese woodblock print, from Moronobu and Harunobu to Utamaro, Sharaku, Hokusai, Hiroshige and Yoshitoshi, in a short illustrated guide.
ldDescription: A short guide to recognizing Japanese woodblock prints (ukiyo-e), 1680s to 1880s, compiled from museum collection records.
